_readme: The specimen pool. Each day the game picks 3 specimens from it.
clue: shown before the answer, so it must not give the age or the answer away.
added: the date (YYYY-MM-DD, UTC) the specimen joins the pool. Days before that date never use it.
Ages are in millions of years ago (Mya). ageRangeMya is the 'spot on' window.
image: path to the photo in assets/. photo: who took it, the licence, and the page it came from. Every photo must have one.
Safe to do: add new specimens with today's date or later, and fix typos or facts.
Never do (after launch): delete a specimen, change an id, or change an 'added' date. Past days would change.
Entries marked example: true were the first starter content. Every entry has a source link for checking its facts.

specimens.name: Trilobite (Elrathia kingii)
specimens.clue: A small, ridged, bug-like shape pressed into dark grey shale.
specimens.foundIn: Wheeler Shale, House Range, Utah, USA
specimens.fact: One of the most common trilobite fossils in the world. Trilobites were sea animals related to insects and crabs, and they lasted for nearly 300 million years.

specimens.name: Ammonite (Dactylioceras commune)
specimens.clue: A tightly coiled, ribbed shell, about 7 cm across.
specimens.fact: Local legend said Saint Hilda turned Whitby's snakes to stone. Victorian sellers carved snake heads onto ammonites like this one and sold them as 'snakestones'.

specimens.name: Tyrannosaurus rex tooth
specimens.clue: A long, curved tooth with a smooth tip and a cracked, crumbly root.
specimens.fact: T. rex replaced its teeth throughout its life, which is why shed teeth are among the more common T. rex finds. This one is at the Museum of the Rockies in Montana.

specimens.name: Megalodon tooth (Otodus megalodon)
specimens.clue: A huge triangular tooth with fine serrations, as wide as a hand.
specimens.fact: Megalodon was a giant shark. Its teeth could grow up to about 18 cm long, and sharks shed thousands of teeth in a lifetime, so they turn up often.

specimens.name: Fly in Baltic amber
specimens.clue: A tiny fly trapped inside a polished lump of clear yellow resin.
specimens.fact: Amber is fossilised tree resin. Sticky resin trapped insects so quickly that some still show tiny hairs and wing veins.

specimens.name: Seed fern leaf (Neuropteris flexuosa)
specimens.clue: A row of fern-like leaflets printed on a slab of dark rock.
specimens.fact: It looks like a fern, but Neuropteris was a seed fern: a plant that made seeds instead of spores. Forests of plants like this became today's coal.

specimens.name: Woolly mammoth tooth
specimens.clue: A heavy, brick-sized block with ridged plates along its top.
specimens.fact: Woolly mammoths ground up tough grass with teeth like this one, made of ridged plates of enamel. Like elephants, they went through six sets of molars in a lifetime.

specimens.name: Manganese dendrites
specimens.clue: Delicate black branching fronds spread across pale limestone.
specimens.fact: Not a plant at all. Mineral-rich water seeped into cracks in the rock and left manganese oxide crystals that grew in branching, fern-like patterns.

specimens.name: Chambered nautilus shell
specimens.clue: A coiled shell cut in half, showing a spiral of chambers inside.
specimens.fact: Nautiluses are still alive today. Their shells look a lot like ammonites, which died out with the dinosaurs 66 million years ago.

photo.author: Eric A. Lazo-Wasem, Yale Peabody Museum

specimens.name: Fake trilobite in a 'nodule'
specimens.clue: A stone nodule split open, with a trilobite on each half.
specimens.foundIn: Bought from a rock and fossil seller
specimens.fact: Everything about this is fake: it isn't rock and it isn't a fossil. The whole thing was moulded to look like a natural nodule split open. Fakes like this, and much more convincing ones, are sold to collectors and tourists.

specimens.name: Beringer's 'lying stones'
specimens.clue: Three flat stones, each with a creature standing out on its surface.
specimens.foundIn: A hillside near Würzburg, Germany, in 1725
specimens.fact: Professor Johann Beringer published a book about these 'fossils'. They had been carved and planted by colleagues who wanted to embarrass him.

specimens.name: Archaeopteryx (Berlin specimen)
specimens.clue: A small skeleton with feathered wings and a long bony tail, spread across pale limestone.
specimens.fact: Half bird, half dinosaur: it had feathers and wings, but also teeth, clawed fingers and a long bony tail. For over a century it was thought to be the oldest known bird.

specimens.name: Sabre-toothed cat skull (Smilodon populator)
specimens.clue: A big cat's skull with two enormous, blade-like upper fangs.
specimens.fact: Not a tiger: Smilodon belonged to a separate, extinct branch of cats. Its name means 'scalpel tooth', and it was first named in 1842 from fossils found in Brazil.

specimens.name: Giant deer skeleton (Megaloceros giganteus)
specimens.clue: A deer skeleton taller than a person, with huge, flat, spreading antlers.
specimens.fact: Also called the Irish elk, though it wasn't an elk. Its antlers could span over 4 metres, the biggest of any known deer, and some survived until about 7,700 years ago.

specimens.name: Glyptodon (giant armadillo relative)
specimens.clue: A huge dome-shaped shell made of bony plates, as big as a small car.
specimens.fact: A giant relative of armadillos. Its fossils were first found in Uruguay in 1814, but early scientists mistook them for a giant ground sloth.

specimens.name: Fossil herring (Knightia)
specimens.clue: A small fish skeleton, every bone visible, on smooth pale stone.
specimens.fact: The most commonly dug-up fossil fish in the world, and the state fossil of Wyoming. It was related to modern herrings.

specimens.name: Bat (Palaeochiropteryx tupaiodon)
specimens.clue: A tiny skeleton with long finger bones folded at its sides, on orange-brown shale.
specimens.fact: Fossils from the Messel Pit are so well preserved that some of these early bats still show the outlines of their fur, ears and wing skin.

specimens.name: Nummulites (giant single-celled shells)
specimens.clue: A handful of flat, coin-shaped stone discs, from pea-sized to larger than a coin.
specimens.foundIn: Near Al Ain, United Arab Emirates
specimens.fact: Each 'coin' was the shell of a single-celled sea creature. Limestones packed with them are common around the Mediterranean, including in Egypt.

specimens.name: Microraptor (four-winged dinosaur)
specimens.clue: A crow-sized skeleton with a long tail and a faint halo of feathers around it.
specimens.fact: Microraptor had feathered wings on its arms and its legs, giving it four wings. It was a small relative of Velociraptor.

specimens.name: Heart urchin (Micraster decipiens)
specimens.clue: A heart-shaped stone with a five-pointed star pattern on top.
specimens.fact: A sea urchin that lived buried in the sea floor, drawing in water through the groove at the front of its shell.

specimens.name: Ammolite (Placenticeras ammonite shell)
specimens.clue: A polished oval of rainbow colours, set like a gemstone.
specimens.fact: This gemstone is a fossil: the rainbow layer is ammonite shell. It's one of the few gems made by living things, along with amber and pearl.

specimens.name: Ichthyosaurs (Stenopterygius)
specimens.clue: A dolphin-shaped skeleton outlined in dark rock, with a smaller one swimming below it.
specimens.fact: Ichthyosaurs were sea reptiles shaped like dolphins. One Stenopterygius fossil shows a mother that died giving birth, with her baby coming out tail-first, like a whale's.

specimens.name: 'Devil's toenail' oyster (Gryphaea arcuata)
specimens.clue: A thick, grey, curled-over shell about the size of a golf ball.
specimens.fact: People once carried these fossil oysters to ward off rheumatism. Their curled shape earned them the name 'devil's toenails'.

specimens.name: Petrified log
specimens.clue: A cross-section of a tree trunk that has turned into colourful stone.
specimens.foundIn: Petrified Forest National Park, Arizona, USA
specimens.fact: Minerals slowly replaced the wood, keeping the shape of the trunk and even its rings. The park in Arizona is named after its huge numbers of these logs.

specimens.name: Mesosaurus
specimens.clue: A slender reptile skeleton with a long tail and a narrow snout, on pale grey rock.
specimens.fact: A small reptile that lived in water, yet its fossils turn up in both southern Africa and South America. That was early evidence that the two continents were once joined.

specimens.name: Scale tree bark (Lepidodendron)
specimens.clue: Dark rock covered in neat, diamond-shaped scales, like snakeskin.
specimens.fact: Not snakeskin: it's bark from a scale tree, which could grow 50 metres tall. Swampy forests of them helped form much of the world's coal.

specimens.name: Tully monster (Tullimonstrum)
specimens.clue: A stone nodule split in two, with a strange cigar-shaped creature printed inside.
specimens.fact: Scientists still argue about what it was. It has been compared to molluscs, worms, arthropods and fish. It has only ever been found at Mazon Creek in Illinois.

specimens.name: Trilobite (Phacops)
specimens.clue: A rounded, bumpy, bug-like creature with big eyes made of many tiny lenses.
specimens.fact: Phacops often rolled up into a ball for protection, like a woodlouse, and many are found curled up that way.

specimens.name: Petoskey stone (fossil coral)
specimens.clue: A smooth, polished pebble covered in a pattern of six-sided cells.
specimens.fact: It's a fossil coral colony. Ice-age glaciers plucked pieces from the bedrock and ground them into pebbles, which collectors now hunt for in Michigan.

specimens.name: Sea scorpion (Eurypterus remipes)
specimens.clue: A scorpion-like creature with paddle-shaped legs and a long spiky tail.
specimens.fact: Eurypterus makes up more than 95% of all sea scorpion fossils ever found, and it is the state fossil of New York.

specimens.name: 'Dudley bug' trilobite (Calymene blumenbachii)
specimens.clue: A small trilobite with a big rounded head, lying on grey limestone.
specimens.fact: So many were found in the limestone quarries of Dudley that it appeared on the town's coat of arms, earning the nickname the 'Dudley bug'.

specimens.name: Isotelus (giant trilobite)
specimens.clue: A big, smooth, oval trilobite with faint segments, on pale stone.
specimens.fact: The state fossil of Ohio. Isotelus holds the record for the largest trilobite fossil ever found, at over 70 cm long.

specimens.name: Marrella splendens
specimens.clue: A tiny feathery creature with long sweeping spines, like a shadow on dark shale.
specimens.fact: The most common animal in the Burgess Shale: tens of thousands have been collected. A dark stain is often preserved around it.

specimens.name: Dickinsonia
specimens.clue: An oval imprint with fine ribs running out from a line down its middle.
specimens.fact: One of the oldest known animals, from before the Cambrian. It lived on shallow sea floors, feeding on mats of microbes.

specimens.name: Septarian nodule
specimens.clue: A smooth dark stone crossed by cracks filled with pale crystal, like a tortoise shell.
specimens.fact: Not a turtle or a dinosaur egg: it's a concretion, a lump of mineral that hardened inside mud. It cracked as it shrank, and the cracks later filled with crystal.

specimens.name: Moqui marbles
specimens.clue: Two dark, round balls, one cracked open to show sand inside.
specimens.fact: These iron-coated sandstone balls look like fossil eggs, but they formed when iron-rich groundwater flowed through the rock. They're named after a Hopi legend.

specimens.name: Fulgurite ('fossilised lightning')
specimens.clue: A rough, hollow tube of fused sand, like a stone branch or a fossil burrow.
specimens.fact: Made by lightning, not by life. When lightning strikes sand it can melt it into a glassy tube in a split second.

specimens.name: Atlantic horseshoe crab shell
specimens.clue: A helmet-shaped brown shell with a long spiked tail, lying on pebbles.
specimens.foundIn: A beach in Rhode Island, USA
specimens.fact: Horseshoe crabs are still alive today and look much like fossils of their ancient relatives. Despite the name, they're more closely related to spiders than to crabs.

specimens.name: Insects in copal
specimens.clue: A glowing orange lump with tiny bugs and bubbles trapped inside.
specimens.fact: Copal is tree resin that has hardened but hasn't had time to become amber. It's often sold as amber, but the insects inside aren't ancient.

specimens.name: Cast of the London Archaeopteryx
specimens.clue: A feathered skeleton with spread wings, pressed into a flat grey slab.
specimens.fact: A copy of the famous Archaeopteryx in London's Natural History Museum. Museums share casts of rare fossils so more people can see them.

specimens.name: Piltdown Man
specimens.clue: A human-like skull with a heavy, ape-like jaw.
specimens.fact: Presented in 1912 as a missing link between apes and humans. It was really a human skull and an orangutan jaw, stained to look old. The hoax was exposed in 1953.
